extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, researchers, and students interested in media ethics and legal investigations
extracted.subtask_description: A topical encyclopedia-style overview summarising the history, investigations, legal issues, institutional responses, and consequences of phone-hacking by news organisations (primarily UK-focused, 1990s–2012). Intended to inform readers about events, actors, evidence, and procedural outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criminality under the Computer Misuse Act 1990
rubrics_metrics.description: Hacking was illegal under the 1990 Computer Misuse Act regardless of whether messages had already been listened to by their intended recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that although the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) initially gave narrow guidance on charging, the Computer Misuse Act made the activities criminal regardless of the victim's prior listening; this distinction affected the CPS/Met decisions about prosecutions and scope of inquiry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article states that interception might not have been an offence under the 2000 Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act in some circumstances, which affected early CPS advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CPS advice and legal interpretations about which statutory regimes applied (CMA vs RIPA) influenced whether police considered certain acts prosecutable; disputes over this guidance later became the subject of public disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: CPS charging guidance regarding interception offences
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted CPS rationale: 'phone hacking was only an offence if messages had been intercepted before they were listened to by the intended recipient.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This interpretation was used to limit the scope of early investigations; the article documents that this CPS position and its use by the Met were controversial and later disputed when broader evidence emerged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press Complaints Commission (PCC) stance on subterfuge and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: PCC 2007/2009 guidance: there is 'a legitimate place for the use of subterfuge when there are grounds in the public interest to use it and it is not possible to obtain information through other means.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article records criticism of the PCC for being industry-funded and for producing guidance the Information Commissioner described as 'disappointing'; the PCC's conclusions (and later withdrawal) influenced debates about self-regulation and acceptable newsgathering methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigative thoroughness, disclosure, and avoidance of conflicts of interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigations should examine available evidence comprehensively, notify victims, question implicated reporters/executives, and avoid conflicts of interest between police and press.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents numerous failures: evidence stored 'in garbage bags', limited interviews, narrow focus on a few victims, senior officers' social ties with editors, failure to disclose documents to CPS, and delayed database entry of seized materials — all cited as departures from proper investigative/prosecutorial standards that impeded accountability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for internal corporate/legal inquiries
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal or commissioned inquiries must have sufficiently broad mandates and transparent disclosure to determine whether wrongdoing was systemic rather than limited to a 'rogue reporter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article describes how News International engaged firms (Burton Copeland, Linklaters, Harbottle & Lewis) with constrained mandates, limited email selection, no waiver of privilege, and omissions (e.g., not reviewing cash payments or certain email traffic), producing reports that were subsequently criticised as inadequate for establishing corporate responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal methods of acquiring confidential information (types of wrongdoing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Documented illegal methods included accessing private voicemail accounts, hacking computers, making false statements to officials, entrapment, blackmail, burglaries, theft of mobile phones, and making payments to officials in exchange for confidential information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists these methods as the factual substance of alleged criminality across multiple publications and private investigators; recognizing these as distinct modes of illegal acquisition was central to investigations, civil suits, and regulatory scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Victim redress and civil litigation standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Victims retained solicitors and filed civil suits for invasion of privacy, sometimes receiving substantial financial payments; settlement practices (including gagging provisions) affected public disclosure of evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil claims and settlements are described as a critical mechanism that produced disclosures (leaked settlement details, documents) which in turn prompted wider investigative reporting and extended inquiries; the article highlights that sealed files and gagging terms impeded public awareness of the scale of wrongdoing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media accountability and public statements (truthfulness to oversight bodies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives’ statements to Parliamentary committees, regulators, and the public must accurately reflect known evidence; misleading testimony or cover-up undermines accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article documents examples where News International executives and others presented the hacking as the work of a single 'rogue reporter,' despite documentary evidence to the contrary; such misrepresentations fueled criticism and were central to calls for inquiries (e.g., Leveson) and institutional reforms.
